items.title: A ‘Generational Clash’ Is Fueling Europe’s Protests
items.summary: As retirees live longer, governments need to spend more on pensions. That makes it harder to fund other services, spurring protests like those in France.
items.full_text: Sébastien Ducros, a French data analyst who supports the widespread student protests in his country, has identified an obvious culprit for the lack of government funds for dilapidated schools. “A huge portion of the money is going toward retirees, while many other things are being neglected,” said Mr. Ducros, 36. “I honestly think — even if it feels strange to say — that people like my parents are in a position where they should and could” surrender some of their pension payments, he added, saying that they were about to retire. But Laurent Grinwald, 72, who retired recently after decades as a postal worker, isn’t eager for his pension to be reduced, particularly to pay for other state-funded services. Especially, he said, as rents and the cost of living have shot up. “We’ve been working all this time,” Mr. Grinwald said, “and now, suddenly, the stance is, ‘Well, no, we’re going to start taking a bit more?’” This disagreement embodies a broader question for Europe, one at the heart of the mass antigovernment demonstrations that returned to France on Saturday, as well as recent protests driven by frustrated young people in countries including Belgium, Germany, Greece, Italy and Portugal. As Europeans live longer, should the needs of the young be eclipsed by their parents’ and grandparents’ pensions, routinely the largest items in Europe’s national budgets? “It’s a generational clash,” said Jorge Galindo, the director of EsadeEcPol, an independent think tank in Spain, which has some of the most generous pensions in Europe. items.title: ‘Get Focused on London’: How Iran’s Agents Attacked European Targets
items.summary: A wave of assaults in Britain and elsewhere in the spring sowed fear across Europe. Prosecutors shed new light on how Iran took aim at U.S. allies.
items.full_text: As the U.S.-Israel war in Iran raged earlier this year, a man linked to Iranian criminal networks perched in front of a computer, on a video call with a teenager in London. The man wanted to make sure the teen, who was moments away from setting fire to a synagogue, carried out his plans. “Light it up like a Christmas tree,” the man, an Iraqi named Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, urged the 17-year-old, according to U.S. prosecutors. The teen climbed over a wall and tossed a bomb through a broken window. “J’s mic is muted,” read the text on Mr. al-Hassani’s computer screen. The synagogue arson in April was a small, violent part of Iran’s efforts to force an end to the bombing campaign that was pummeling the country, according to American investigators. The attack was described in a federal indictment filed in New York this week. It revealed extensive new details about a wave of violence against Jewish institutions in Europe and U.S. targets, including a British air base used by American bombers. Prosecutors hold Iran’s agents responsible for the assaults. Within days of the war starting, Mr. al-Hassani and at least two associates, including an operative for Iran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, began plotting the attacks in Europe, prosecutors said. The men talked about procuring drones and missiles from contacts in Iran. They pored over a map of London, with one saying they should “get focused” on targeting the British capital. Soon after, attacks hit temples and other Jewish sites in London. In the fight against much stronger conventional forces, Iran has found ways to impose costs on its adversaries without inviting a full military response. One major aspect of Iran’s strategy is its embrace of small-time criminals to conduct low-cost assaults against vulnerable targets that are part of everyday life. items.title: Ukraine’s Starshield Access Is Being Restricted Again, Zelensky Says
items.summary: President Volodymyr Zelensky said the system, which Ukraine uses to guide drones, was being throttled over Russian-occupied territory. SpaceX, its developer, has denied the claim.
items.full_text: Ukrainian military operations were disrupted again this week along the front lines because of restrictions on Starshield, the satellite internet system developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX and controlled by the U.S. government, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday. Mr. Zelensky told reporters that speed limits of about 100 miles per hour were being enforced for Ukrainian devices connected to the system. It would be the second time in recent weeks that Ukraine’s Starshield connectivity had been throttled. The previous restrictions caused Ukrainian drones to lose their connection to the system if they flew above certain speeds. Mr. Zelensky said that the latest speed limits took effect on Monday and were being enforced over Russian-occupied territories, not over all of Ukraine. That hurts Ukraine’s ability to strike Russian troops with drones in those territories. Imposing restrictions on occupied territories is “very dangerous, because it already has political implications,” Mr. Zelensky said. “If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognizing the temporarily occupied territories as not ours,” he added. Mr. Zelensky said separately in his nightly speech that the Starshield limits hurt Ukraine’s ability to use newly developed interceptors to protect its cities from Russia’s jet-powered drones . It is likely, however, that those limits would not affect interceptors in Kyiv, the capital, which is being battered by jet-powered drones but is far from the front lines. Mr. Musk and SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment on Friday evening. SpaceX had earlier told Axios that the Ukrainian claim about throttled connectivity was false. items.title: Trump’s Oil Grab in Venezuela Is Testing the Country’s National Identity
items.summary: Long-held beliefs in Venezuela about sovereign control over oil are fraying as the U.S. lays claim to the country’s oil reserves.
items.full_text: Like generations before him, Leonardo Silva grew up steeped in beliefs about the extraordinarily abundant resource that made Venezuela special. All the oil under their feet was theirs, they felt. Virtually free gasoline was a birthright. To be born atop this bounty was like winning the lottery. Mr. Silva, 38, said his generation viewed oil as a cornerstone of the country’s national identity, when a booming economy allowed Venezuela to occupy a privileged tier in the global order. His children, he said, have a far less rosy view. “To them oil isn’t important, it’s secondary,” said Mr. Silva, who works at a foundation in Caracas helping people with disabilities. “They don’t have that culture of us being a rich country. They just know that if you don’t work, you don’t eat.” Oil has shaped Venezuela to an extent that is rare outside the Middle East for more than a century, becoming a defining feature of the social fabric like baseball , beauty pageants or the veneration of the liberation hero Simón Bolívar. But now the U.S. government is taking control of a huge portion of Venezuela’s oil. And, pressed by economic need, long-held nationalist convictions about oil, starting with the need for sovereign control, are giving way to a more complex web of perspectives. The ways in which Venezuelans are re-evaluating oil, and by extension their reliance on it, are the result of immense upheaval over the last decade. Oil production plummeted because of mismanagement, political purges, corruption and sanctions. Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: South Sudan’s National Election, Its First, Will Be Delayed
items.summary: Analysts had warned that the vote, originally set for December, faced a legitimacy crisis. South Sudan has not held a national election since gaining independence in 2011.
items.full_text: Officials in South Sudan, the world’s youngest state, said on Saturday that its first national election would be postponed, raising new questions about a vote that analysts had already said could not yield a credible result. The National Elections Commission said in a statement that the presidential and legislative elections, which had been scheduled for Dec. 22, would be held on Feb. 11 instead. The country’s information minister, Ateny Wek Ateny, said the postponement would allow more time to register voters and educate them about the process. South Sudan has never held a national election. Since gaining independence from Sudan in 2011 after decades of war, it has been ruled by President Salva Kiir, and it has faced seemingly intractable political difficulties. In 2013, civil war broke out between the government and forces loyal to the main opposition leader, Riek Machar. Under a peace agreement to end the conflict in 2018, Mr. Machar became the vice president in a transitional government. The upcoming election was supposed to underwrite that agreement. But the peace deal has unraveled since March 2025, when Mr. Machar was placed under house arrest in the capital, Juba, and charged with treason. In recent months, the government has replaced opposition lawmakers with its own supporters and dissolved the unity government. With Mr. Machar effectively sidelined, there are no credible challengers to Mr. Kiir, who is widely expected to win the presidential election. He has a broad national following, and his party controls state institutions and the news media. The election faces stark logistical challenges. Civil servants have not been paid in more than a year, and parts of the country are controlled by armed groups, including Mr. Machar’s forces. Thousands of people have died in fighting and attacks on civilians. In March, more than 200 people were killed in a massacre in Unity State near the border with Sudan, according to human rights groups. “The conditions for credible polls are not currently in place,” the International Crisis Group said in a briefing for the U.N. Security Council this week. “Rushed elections could be a decisive final blow to the 2018 framework and would open the door to a return to sustained large-scale violence.” Mr. Ateny, the information minister, acknowledged that the government could not gain access to “small parts” of the country, but said the election would be credible. “It’s not always 100 percent, but it can be good for the sovereignty of the country and it’s good for the mandate of the state,” he said in an interview. In addition to the violence and civil unrest, South Sudanese have been faced with soaring food prices, drought and flooding. Of the country’s roughly 12 million people, more than 8 million are in need of food assistance, according to the Famine Early Warning Systems Network, a globally recognized monitor of hunger.

items.title: Two Celebrity Cases Put a Spotlight on British Courts’ Gag Orders
items.summary: Russell Brand and the TV personality David Walliams both persuaded courts to suppress misconduct allegations against them. Some say the libel laws need to change.
items.full_text: Two recent cases have brought new attention to the ways that British laws can allow the wealthy and powerful to silence their critics. The first was the rape and sexual assault trial of the comedian Russell Brand. Before his conviction last week, Mr. Brand had obtained an injunction prohibiting another accuser from telling almost anyone — including the police, her family and most doctors — about her claims that he assaulted her. (Mr. Brand has denied her allegations.) That injunction, first revealed by Dan Neidle, a tax lawyer and free-expression activist, apparently remains in force. In the second instance, two British news organizations were temporarily blocked from reporting allegations of sexual misconduct against David Walliams, a television personality and author of children’s books, before a judge declined to make the injunction permanent. The Guardian newspaper and ITV News, a British broadcaster, published investigations last week into the allegations, which Mr. Walliams denies. Though both men now face public scrutiny, the revelations of how they used court injunctions — essentially gag orders — to protect their reputations have provoked no shortage of public and political outrage. Judges in other cases have issued “super injunctions,” which prohibit publishing any information even about the injunction itself. “What will the government do to prevent these abuses of process, and stop the abusive injunctions and super injunctions which stop scrutiny, accountability and the work of the free press?” Nick Timothy, the shadow justice minister, asked in Parliament on Tuesday. The British government is now “looking at what we can do,” Alex Davies-Jones, the government minister responsible for victims of crime and violence against women and girls, said in response. items.title: Eisenkot Accuses Netanyahu of Fueling ‘Racist’ Hostility Against Arabs
items.summary: Gadi Eisenkot sharply criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu days after the Israeli leader attacked Arab lawmakers in a divisive speech.
items.full_text: Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who is trying to form the next Israeli government, accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday of fueling a “racist” campaign against the country’s Arab citizens, in some of the strongest public criticism of his rival’s attacks on the community. The comments were made days after Mr. Netanyahu delivered a divisive speech to the opening session of Parliament, or the Knesset, in which he referred to Arab lawmakers as “terror supporters” and “haters of Israel.” Diplomats and analysts condemned the remarks as a brazen display of hatred and incitement against Arab citizens, who make up about 20 percent of the overall population, and voted in massive numbers in inconclusive elections last month. “Since the beginning of the election campaign, they have been subjected to a racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimization, fueled by the outgoing prime minister and those around him for political purposes,” Mr. Eisenkot said in a statement on social media. “Arab citizens of Israel are an integral part of the Israeli story,” he said, adding that it was wrong to malign an entire community. “The attempt to marginalize them and vilify them collectively is a profound violation of the principles of statesmanship,” Mr. Eisenkot said. “It dishonors Israel’s Declaration of Independence and the values we take pride in as a Jewish and democratic state.” The Declaration of Independence says all citizens have equal social and political rights “irrespective of religion, race or sex.” Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: Caught Between Killers: Ebola on One Side, Islamic State on the Other
items.summary: The new epicenter of Congo’s fast-spreading outbreak is a region scarred by rebel violence. Responders are struggling to help it.
items.full_text: Six months on, Ebola continues to hack a deadly trail across eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. When the outbreak was first detected in May, it resembled a single, giant blaze, with infections concentrated in a handful of towns in one province. It has since morphed into a far bigger, more elusive foe, creeping into eight provinces and splintering into numerous hot spots as it moves through one of the world’s great rainforests. Instead of one big fire, there are many now, scattered across a vast area about the size of Britain. Health workers have corralled the virus where it was first detected, but infections are soaring elsewhere. Biakato, a small town deep in the rainforest, suddenly accounted for as many as one-quarter of new cases nationally. Yet its beleaguered residents were left almost entirely on their own, with dangerously little to defend themselves against the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history . “We see the same mistakes as before,” said Dr. Jean-Jacques Muyembe, who helped discover Ebola in 1976 and now heads Congo’s National Institute for Biomedical Research. “It’s as if we were starting from zero. It’s very disappointing.” And if that were not enough, the campaign to contain the epidemic has run into a terrifying new threat: the Islamic State.

items.title: The U.S.-Israel Relationship Is Broken. Here’s How Eisenkot Could Fix It.
items.summary: Former Israeli and U.S. ambassadors, lawmakers and analysts largely agree on steps Gadi Eisenkot could take if he becomes prime minister. But they are risky.
items.full_text: Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who has been given a chance to form Israel’s new governing coalition and replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is by no means assured of success. But if he does take power, another hugely daunting challenge would immediately confront him: how to undo the vast damage done to Israel’s relationship with the United States, its closest and most important ally. It’s hard to imagine things getting much worse. Many Americans have turned against Israel over its devastating military campaign in Gaza, and even more so over its role in pressing for war with Iran , which led to soaring gas prices. President Trump announced this month that he would cut off billions of dollars in annual U.S. military aid to Israel by the end of the year and blamed Israel in part for Republican losses in the midterm elections. Democratic control of Congress could quickly lead to sanctions on violent Israeli settlers and on new settlement construction in the occupied West Bank, as well as to new conditions on arms sales. In the past, Israel could always turn to Congress for support in clashes with the White House, said Michael Oren, a former Israeli ambassador to Washington and deputy prime minister under Mr. Netanyahu. But no longer. “For the first time in the history of our relationship with the United States, we have no recourse,” he said. “We have to start from scratch. We have a lot of fence mending to do and with no guarantee of success. Zero.” Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: Study Hard, Get a Career and Get Ahead? It’s Not What It Used to Be.
items.summary: From India to France, the implicit meritocratic bargain that underwrote stable societies by providing advancement to new generations is breaking down.
items.full_text: Protest movements have long relied on students as some of the most ardent foot soldiers. Young people have been on the front lines of protests against war, climate change and racial inequality. But in huge protests that have shaken India and France this fall, students have revolted against the failed promises of education itself. In India, students took to the streets after the government abruptly canceled the results of a medical-school admissions exam because test questions had been leaked online. Aspiring doctors had to take the test again, after many spent years studying for up to 12 hours a day in hopes of winning one of the coveted spots — and the chance of upward mobility. Young people across the country saw the scandal as emblematic of a broken education system and were furious. In France, students in poor suburbs outside Paris began protesting the decrepit physical condition of their schools, an opaque university admissions system and absent teachers. French education had long promised to serve as a “social elevator” enabling young people to advance in society, but had fallen into disrepair. Soon, demonstrations spread across the country and, in some cities, spiraled into rioting. In both countries, the anger of the students shows no signs of abating. And while in many ways France and India could hardly be more different, their unrest was sparked by a similar source of outrage: the breakdown of a foundational social contract that one could call the meritocratic bargain. It is a promise that lies at the core of many countries’ political compacts. Though specifics can vary, the central proposition usually goes something like this: A fair society rewards merit. Educational achievements are a good measure of merit because education is open to all and leads to valuable skills. Therefore, education should be a route to social and economic advancement. The value of this system is not just that it selects for those with high ability, but also that it offers a justification for the resulting socioeconomic hierarchy — including who ends up at the bottom. “All selection mechanisms generate losers,” said Nicholas Kuipers, a professor at Princeton University who studies the politics of meritocracy. “The question is, Who do you want to be a loser, and who do you want to be a winner?” Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: SpaceX Makes History With Successful Rocket Catch in Texas
items.summary: The Starship spacecraft returned from orbit to the same spot where it lifted off, marking a key milestone in SpaceX’s vision of building fully reusable rockets.
items.full_text: SpaceX’s giant Starship spacecraft pulled off a remarkable feat on Saturday afternoon in the quest to build fully reusable rockets. For the first time, the spacecraft successfully returned from orbit to its launch site in South Texas, where it was caught between two mechanical arms on the launch tower. For the past decade, SpaceX has successfully landed the boosters of its smaller Falcon 9 rockets and then reused them on subsequent launches. But the upper stages of the Falcon 9s are still thrown away each time. The Starship rocket system is not only much larger than Falcon 9, but it was designed from the start to be fully reusable. Bringing back an upper stage from orbit is a major technical hurdle, and SpaceX was able to pull it off on its first try. Jared Isaacman, the NASA administrator, offered his congratulations on X . “Making more believers by the day….one step closer to,” he wrote, adding an emoji of the moon and the American flag. Starship is slated to serve as one of two lander designs that will take astronauts to the surface of the moon as part of NASA’s Artemis program. Elon Musk, the chief executive of SpaceX, posted a video on X showing a view of Starship from below, part of the post-landing inspection. A few hours earlier, the spacecraft, which is about 170 feet long, had been traveling at more than 17,000 miles per hour at an altitude of 170 miles. Then, one of its engines fired briefly, nudging it out of orbit to begin its fall back to Earth. Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: Family Dollar to Pay $63 Million Settlement for Overcharging Customers
items.summary: Since 2023, the discount retailer has been overcharging shoppers “millions of dollars” at checkout, according to a complaint filed by federal regulators and 17 states.
items.full_text: Family Dollar has agreed to pay a $63 million settlement after federal and state authorities filed complaints against the company for charging customers more than amounts advertised in mailers and displayed on store shelves. The settlement, which was announced by the Federal Trade Commission on Thursday, came alongside a same-day order , filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia. The order seeks to prevent the retailer from continuing its deceptive pricing practices and would require it to create a “pricing accuracy program,” to be independently certified on an annual basis. “Today’s order will ensure Family Dollar stops deceiving consumers about its prices and returns money to consumers harmed by these practices,” Christopher Mufarrige, the director of the F.T.C.’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in the announcement. The agreement is the result of a complaint filed by the commission and 17 states on Thursday, which claimed that Family Dollar had overcharged consumers “millions of dollars” since January 2023. The F.T.C. and Family Dollar did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Saturday. In the order, Family Dollar said that it neither admitted to nor denied any of the allegations in the complaint. Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: She Was a CBS News Producer When Few Women Were
items.summary: Linda Mason started in an entry-level job at CBS Radio in 1966 and rose through the news division’s ranks to senior vice president. She was 84.
items.full_text: Linda Mason, an Emmy Award-winning journalist at CBS News who was the first female producer at “CBS Evening News” with Walter Cronkite and who was put in charge of reinforcing the division’s standards after a botched “60 Minutes” report on President George W. Bush’s military service, died on Oct. 28 at her home in the Bronx. She was 84. Her husband, Cary Aminoff, said the cause was dementia. Ms. Mason stood out for her long rise through the male-dominated news division. She started as a desk assistant at CBS Radio before moving into jobs of increasing responsibility, including senior producer of “CBS Evening News”; executive producer of “CBS News Sunday Morning” and the documentary news series “CBS Reports”; and vice president of public affairs, developing programming and overseeing standards. She was also known as a mentor to other women at the network. “We took it for granted that every woman was going to be a secretary or a researcher, and she had made it to the exalted position of producer,” Marcy McGinnis, who started at CBS News as a secretary and later became a producer and senior vice president of news coverage, said in an interview. “I looked to her as my North Star. Oh, I wanted to be like her. And she was nice to me and other people like me who didn’t matter at the time.” In 2004, as a vice president, Ms. Mason was CBS News’s liaison to an independent review panel convened by the network to investigate a flawed “60 Minutes Wednesday” report about Mr. Bush, which was broadcast two months before his successful campaign for re-election. It purported to raise serious questions about the president’s Vietnam-era Texas Air National Guard service and whether he had received preferential treatment because of his family’s political connections. Her role was to answer questions from the panel — led by Louis D. Boccardi, a former chief executive of The Associated Press, and Dick Thornburgh, a former attorney general of the United States — about CBS’s reporting methods. “For months, I felt as if I were in isolation, quarantined,” she wrote in her memoir, “Speak Up: Breaking the Glass Ceiling at CBS News” (2023). “It was a very difficult time for me since I was used to being involved in all the events CBS was covering and talking with my colleagues.” Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: How Some Flights Were Exempt From the Ground Stop
items.summary: Dozens of international flights departed from the United States during Friday’s nationwide ground stop. Some planes also left for Hawaii from the West Coast.
items.full_text: Thousands of passengers scrambled to update their travel plans on Saturday as air traffic slowly unsnarled after a nationwide ground stop on Friday, but a number of travelers had already arrived at their destinations on flights left unaffected by the order. Dozens of international flights took to the skies even as airports across the United States coped with only the third nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration this century. Certain flights were also permitted to depart from the West Coast to Hawaii during the stoppage. Here’s why some air travel was allowed to proceed even as flight systems were hampered. Some international flights were able to depart. More than 8,200 flights were canceled nationwide on Friday — over 31 percent of those scheduled — according to Cirium, an aviation data firm. But more than 60 flights bound for overseas left the United States during the stoppage, according to Flightradar24 , an aviation tracking site. There are 21 air traffic control facilities, 20 in the contiguous United States and one in Alaska, that oversee swaths of regions throughout the country, according to the F.A.A. As some of those centers recovered, flights were “allowed to depart through coordination with the Air Traffic Control System Command Center,” the F.A.A. said in an advisory less than two hours after the ground stop was ordered. items.title: Ground Stop Highlights Chronic Vulnerabilities in Air Traffic System
items.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration’s aging air traffic control infrastructure has had several disruptive failures in recent months, as officials have sought to make upgrades.
items.full_text: The ground stop that brought air travel across the country to a halt Friday evening highlighted persistent weaknesses in the Federal Aviation Administration’s aging air traffic control infrastructure, which has had several disruptive failures in recent months. Two months ago , a circuit failure and severed fiber optic cable caused crippling ground stops and delays at airports along the East Coast. Smaller outages unfolded in October at Raleigh-Durham International Airport in North Carolina and George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston, when contractors accidentally cut into fiber line. The Friday ground stop, which was only the third the F.A.A. has issued this century, eclipsed the fallout of previous air traffic communications equipment failures. Officials said it was prompted by efforts to replace an outdated router, which caused circuits in the national air traffic network to become overloaded and fail, interrupting communication lines between air traffic controllers and pilots. By Saturday, thousands of flights had been canceled, and airports were still crowded with stranded travelers. The recovery will most likely take days, as airlines rebook passengers and reposition planes. Friday’s breakdown, and the earlier episodes, have underscored the structural vulnerabilities that hamper controllers’ ability to safely manage flight traffic, even after improvements. And they have raised questions about whether federal authorities have done enough to create backup systems to prevent disruptive or catastrophic failures. Friday’s incident touched off a blame game in Washington. Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, accused Congress of failing to pony up for systemwide upgrades. items.title: Geopolitics Looms Over Eurovision, but Not Its Asian Edition
items.summary: So far, the contest’s organizers have kept politics offstage. The European edition shows how difficult that can be.
items.full_text: Geopolitics have long intruded on the Eurovision Song Contest. But they were not really a factor as the event prepared to expand into Asia for the first time . That was still true as of Saturday evening, as the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia was about to start in Bangkok. Over the decades, Eurovision organizers have insisted that the contest is nonpolitical. Its organizers impose rules governing lyrics, political symbols and what can be broadcast. Even so, wars and diplomatic disputes have shaped who gets to sing, who stays home and what broadcasters are willing to air. “Politics is why we watch Eurovision,” said Dean Vuletic , a historian of the show at the University of Luxembourg. Here are some examples of geopolitics bleeding into the European edition of the contest: In 2009, less than a year after fighting a war with Russia, the former Soviet republic of Georgia planned to send a disco song called “We Don’t Wanna Put In” to Eurovision. Eurovision’s organizers said that the apparent dig at Vladimir Putin, then Russia’s prime minister, had to go. Georgia pulled out instead of changing it. In 2017, Russia pulled out of the contest in Kyiv after Ukraine barred its singer from entering the country. And five years later, after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Eurovision barred Russia altogether . In 2024, the war in Gaza triggered mass protests over Israel’s participation. A bitter dispute over government influence on voting followed in 2025, and there were boycotts of the contest by five countries in 2026, the biggest crisis in Eurovision’s 70-year history . The 11 Asian countries that sent artists to Saturday’s show have plenty of offstage geopolitical friction. Cambodia, for example, is set to sing in Thailand’s capital less than a year after a border war between the two neighbors killed dozens and displaced hundreds of thousands. As fighting picked up last year, Cambodia withdrew its athletes from the Southeast Asian Games in Thailand, citing safety concerns. Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: 5 Big Questions as C.E.O.s Meet in China
items.summary: President Trump and U.S. tech executives are expected to gather for a major summit in Shenzhen next week. On the agenda: a stalled trade war, expanding export controls, and suspected spy games.
items.full_text: U.S.-Chinese business relations were thrown a curveball ahead of a major C.E.O. summit in Shenzhen, China, next week. On Thursday, Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive of Nvidia after it was revealed that he had affairs with an executive at the company and a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. One of the architects of the artificial intelligence boom, Huang was also perhaps the strongest proponent in Washington for U.S. companies selling A.I. hardware to China — an issue that has become central to the countries’ fraught economic relationship. Huang, who has a close relationship to President Trump, has also promoted open A.I. models, an approach favored by many Chinese firms. China hawks in Congress have already seized on the scandal, using it to push for three bills that would put more restrictions on technology exports to the country. items.title: This Man Stole $9 Million in Gold Bars on the Upper West Side, Police Say
items.summary: The victim, who believed his financial assets had been compromised, was the target of an online fraud scheme and believed he had to buy the precious metal, the authorities said.

It was there, in broad daylight, that two men approached each other on a Wednesday in April 2025. One of the men, a 67-year-old New Yorker, transported a bag of $9 million in gold bars, each one the size of a chocolate bar, that the police said someone online had instructed him to buy and hand over. The man did exactly as he was told, believing that he could secure his financial assets, which an alert on his computer had led him to believe were compromised, the authorities said. The other man took the sack of gold and fled on foot, according to the police. The first man had been the victim of an online fraud. Now, more than a year and a half after the deceit, the New York Police Department is asking for the public’s help in identifying the man who ran off with the gold bars in connection with a grand larceny investigation. Investigators this week released security camera footage and images of the man suspected of taking the bars. Isaac Kahan, the owner of Bullion Trading LLC , a gold and silver dealer in Manhattan’s Diamond District, wondered about the sheer logistics that were involved in the heist. items.title: He Was China’s Man in Panama. Then He Became a Wanted Man.
items.summary: A Chinese businessman arrived in Panama with money and power. Then he sold a port when his luck turned. Now China wants him sent back.
items.full_text: For years, Zhang Liang warned that powerful people in his former homeland, China, would try to drag him back. Then one Saturday morning in July, it happened. In Panama City, two police officers on motorbikes pulled alongside his black Mercedes-Benz and motioned him to stop. A check of his identification turned up an Interpol red notice from the Chinese authorities, who wanted him extradited on charges of embezzling around $300 million. Mr. Zhang, a 44-year-old dealmaker, barely had time to remove his gray suit jacket and wrap it around his head before officers handcuffed him and paraded him before cameras at Interpol’s National Central Bureau in Panama. He has been behind bars ever since. It was a remarkable fall for Mr. Zhang, one that traces the arc of China’s dealings with the West. He went to Panama ready to make deals and help China extend its influence. He oversaw a port project that promised to turn a former U.S. military base near the Panama Canal’s Atlantic entrance into Latin America’s largest container terminal, establishing a base for Chinese interests near one of the world’s busiest trade routes. Today, China’s ruling Communist Party holds much tighter reins on entrepreneurs like Mr. Zhang. At the same time, Panama has been caught in a showdown between the United States and China: President Trump claims that China exercises too much control over the Panama Canal. Mr. Zhang believes he is a pawn in a larger political game — a way for Beijing to regain direct control over key infrastructure he helped build in Panama. items.title: Jensen Huang Carried a Secret for More Than a Year. It Led to His Downfall.
items.summary: Nvidia’s leader said his relationship with a female customer was just about business. But what he was concealing eventually led to his resignation from the company he created.
items.full_text: Jensen Huang was agitated. It was September 2025, and The New York Times had just called his company about a Singaporean data center firm called Megaspeed that had been led by a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, or Huang Le. The Times was reporting that Mr. Huang, the chief executive of the chip maker Nvidia, had a close relationship with her. Mr. Huang, who Nvidia employees say could have a volcanic temper, wanted to know what The Times was insinuating. Though he didn’t deny that he knew the woman, he was bothered by the suggestion that they might be close, people familiar with the discussion said. Nvidia mounted an aggressive defense. Madison Huang, Mr. Huang’s daughter who acted as her father’s chief of staff, pressed the company’s communications team to push back forcefully. They also had reinforcements, a crisis communications firm called Heller. They insisted that Mr. Huang and the woman from Megaspeed just had a business relationship. Over the next 13 months, Mr. Huang stuck with his story, even after The Times reported last month that the U.S. had gathered intelligence showing that Ms. Huang was secretly working with China’s top spy agency. But last weekend, facing new revelations about the relationship, Mr. Huang finally came clean to Nvidia’s general counsel. He had been having an affair with the woman, after all, said the people familiar with the discussions. The relationship with the Megaspeed executive wasn’t Mr. Huang’s only secret. On Wednesday, a Times reporter called Mr. Huang to ask him about a second extramarital relationship. This time, it was an affair with an executive who reported to him. items.title: The Jensen Huang Scandal Has Shocked Even Scandal-Prone Silicon Valley
items.summary: As Jensen Huang abruptly departs, the tech community grapples with an eternal question: Why do the smartest and most successful men so often act so stupidly?
items.full_text: Artificial intelligence promises transcendence. We will ditch our tired and inefficient bodies, say farewell to tedious work and trips to the grocery store. The computer will tend to all human needs and solve all human problems. Well, that was the idea. A.I. was supposed to achieve a new level of reality this month with the public sale of shares of Anthropic, one of the two start-ups that have created and defined this young industry. A trillion-dollar company will be born, yielding billionaires galore. A.I. is the biggest Silicon Valley story ever. But last Sunday it was suddenly pushed aside when the chief executive of the company whose chips are literally powering this intelligence revolution confessed to cheating on his wife with a woman, Alice Huang, who U.S. officials believe was spying for China. By Thursday morning he had resigned, something few thought possible just days earlier. The scandal that took down Nvidia chief Jensen Huang is full of implications for national security and the global A.I. boom. Mr. Huang ranked among Mark Zuckerberg, Steve Jobs, Elon Musk and Bill Gates as tech leaders who were considered by the world to be inseparable from the companies they built. In Silicon Valley, people were mostly just stunned by the news. Those who have been around for a long time, and seen the stretch of territory south of San Francisco evolve from hardware manufacturing to software development to the dot-com frenzy and now the A.I. boom, said they had never seen anything like it. Tech veterans have witnessed amazing ascensions and equally abrupt falls. They have seen abundant arrogance. Fortunes made and fortunes lost in an instant. But there’s something that stands out this time: Transcendence was never supposed to be tawdry. Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: Tech Leaders Rally Behind Jensen Huang
items.summary: In social media posts and letters to Nvidia’s board, Mr. Huang’s billionaire peers described him as a singular leader who could not be replaced at Nvidia.
items.full_text: Many of Silicon Valley’s executives and investors are rallying behind Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday after revelations that he had affairs with an employee and with a woman whom U.S. officials believed to be a spy for China . In social media posts and letters to Nvidia’s board of directors, Mr. Huang’s billionaire peers described him as a singular leader who could not be replaced at Nvidia. Mr. Huang’s exit, they argued, would set the United States back in the artificial intelligence race. And they blamed Nvidia’s board for bowing to pressure. “Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” Elon Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive and the richest person in the world, said in a social media post on Saturday. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.” The support put a spotlight on Nvidia’s role as the linchpin of the A.I. boom and on Mr. Huang’s leadership as the company grew into one of the most valuable in the world. Nvidia, which started making computer chips for video games, now controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips used in the big A.I. projects that are driving the U.S. economy. Along the way, Mr. Huang became Silicon Valley’s consummate dealmaker , turning Nvidia into a central banker for start-ups that needed chips and funding. “We believe the board should avoid a rush to replace Jensen that undermines and thwarts the best interests of shareholders,” Brad Gerstner, the chief executive of Altimeter Capital Management, and Gavin Baker, the chief investment officer of Atreides Management, wrote in a letter sent on Friday. The investors, whose firms are Nvidia shareholders, asked the company’s board to consider “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.” An open letter to Nvidia’s board , titled “Stand With Jensen,” asked the board to reinstall Mr. Huang as chief executive, to conduct an independent investigation and to explain its actions. As of Saturday morning, the letter had nearly 100,000 signatures, including by current and former employees of Nvidia, business partners like Mr. Musk, and start-up leaders and shareholders including Garry Tan, the chief executive of the venture capital firm Y Combinator. items.title: Inside Microsoft’s Rush to Get Back Online After a Global Outage
items.summary: A prolonged outage left many without email and other services, the most recent reminder that the world’s technological underpinnings rely on just a few companies.
items.full_text: Late into the night Thursday, hundreds of Microsoft engineers and top executives were sitting in their darkened offices or home basements, logged into a video conference triaging a nightmare scenario for a technology company. The world still runs on email, and much of that is processed through Microsoft Outlook. For hours, a company outage affected hospitals, schools, businesses and Congressional offices in Washington. Even Microsoft’s own staff couldn’t use email. On the videoconference, Scott Guthrie, the senior most executive overseeing the company’s computing infrastructure, was proposing possible fixes, according to a person familiar with the call who was not authorized to speak publicly. People chewed on fingernails, rubbed their foreheads and debated how to turn off other services to prevent a “stampeding herd” so that as systems come back online, they would not be overwhelmed with new demands and shut back down. By Friday morning, the company had apologized at least twice. It said it determined that the problem stemmed from a recent upgrade to its network, which shut down some servers, and that the systems were steadily improving. “Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage,” the company said in a statement. “While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.” Finally, they had kept the herd at bay. The prolonged and widespread outage was just the most recent reminder that the technological underpinnings of modern life and business are run through just a handful of major companies. And while cyberattacks and malicious actors can target their systems, sometimes the companies learn the hard way that they can introduce devastating flaws when updating or maintaining their own global systems. Hospitals, law enforcement and government agencies and other vital services are often left vulnerable — unable to function for hours or days at a time. items.title: Microsoft’s Global Outage and Fixes: What We Know
items.summary: Disruptions to the company’s email, messaging and other products lasted about 36 hours, hampering companies and services around the world.
items.full_text: Microsoft said early Saturday that it had fully restored its services after a global outage disrupted them for a day and a half, hampering communications and work at schools, government agencies and offices around the world. The problems began on Thursday and cascaded around the world. The company, based in Redmond, Wash., gradually restored service through Friday until declaring an end to one of its most extensive outages of recent times in an update on Saturday around 1 a.m. Eastern time. Here’s what to know. What happened? Outages started disrupting Microsoft tools and apps around noon Eastern time on Thursday and quickly spread to more than 70 countries and territories, affecting millions of users, according to Downdetector , an outage-tracking site. Some of Microsoft’s most popular products, including the email manager Outlook, the workplace messaging and video calling app Teams and the artificial intelligence assistant Copilot, stopped working. Was this a cyberattack? Microsoft said in a statement on Friday that “for now, we can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity.” It added that the problem was “a technical issue not related to cyber or A.I.” agents. Was the F.A.A. ground stop linked to Microsoft? The company said it had no indication that a Federal Aviation Administration ground stop issued late Friday afternoon , which has affected air travel nationwide, was related to the outage. items.title: Jensen Huang’s Resignation From Nvidia Worries the A.I. Start-Up World
items.summary: Mr. Huang championed start-ups, with Nvidia holding $48 billion worth of stakes in 229 private companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, at the end of July.
items.full_text: For years, Jensen Huang was a frequent presence at Silicon Valley start-up events, networking with founders, judging pitch competitions and showing up at “demo” days. The Nvidia chief executive became a godlike figure in the start-up ecosystem, not just because the industry idolized him as one of the world’s most successful entrepreneurs. Mr. Huang, 63, also made it his mission to help start-ups gain a foothold against the industry’s biggest and most powerful tech companies, providing funding and computing power. “As many good ideas as we have, you don’t have all the world’s good ideas,” he said on the Acquired podcast in 2023. So Mr. Huang’s abrupt resignation from Nvidia on Thursday has investors and start-up founders nervous that they have lost a powerful ally. “Nvidia is the central bank of A.I. and all of a sudden, the Fed chairman is out,” said Tomasz Tunguz, an investor at Theory Ventures, which funds young start-ups. Nvidia held $48 billion worth of stakes in 229 private companies, including large stakes in OpenAI and Anthropic, at the end of July, according to securities filings. items.title: Wall Street Braces for Anthropic’s Spending
items.summary: The company’s financial picture may get murky as it deals with employee stock compensation and the growing costs of artificial intelligence.
items.full_text: Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, introduced his artificial intelligence company to potential stock market investors this week with a sublime vision. He predicted the end of cancer and mental illness within a decade, and a transformation of cognitive work. “If we do this right, we can create an age of miracles,” he said in a marketing video for Anthropic’s initial public offering. Wall Street is grappling with how much it may cost to get to utopia. Stock analysts at Goldman Sachs, the investment bank leading Anthropic’s I.P.O., have told investors privately this week that they forecast the company will burn through more than $65 billion next year, and another $41 billion in 2028, said two people familiar with those discussions. Those totals would make Anthropic’s spending among the most aggressive corporate bets on funding the giant A.I. infrastructure build-out. “We are in aggressive investment mode,” Krishna Rao, Anthropic’s chief financial officer, said in the video, without discussing specific spending forecasts. That spending would create a drastically different financial picture than Anthropic has shown recently. The company generated cash from its business in the first nine months of this year, its I.P.O. prospectus shows, a feat in the expensive business of A.I. model development. It has barely spent the $141 billion it raised privately from investors. The listing on Nasdaq, expected next Thursday, could value Anthropic at $1.4 trillion. It would not only cement its status as one of the world’s most prominent companies but hand it additional firepower to help it pull further ahead of well-heeled rivals like OpenAI and Alphabet. The I.P.O. would deliver Anthropic an additional $100 billion to spend, and make it easier to raise even more money to fund those huge commitments. But Anthropic’s public debut will lead to costs that don’t appear today. It said in the prospectus it anticipated about $40 billion of expenses in the coming years tied to preexisting stock grants it has given employees that haven’t yet hit its accounting books. items.title: Why Anthropic’s Dario Amodei Has Angered OpenAI and Other A.I. Peers
items.summary: Dario Amodei, the company’s chief executive, publicly frets about the dangers of artificial intelligence and has made enemies of his peers along the way.
items.full_text: Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, was becoming a nuisance for his fellow technology industry executives. Anthropic and OpenAI, the leading artificial intelligence companies, were lobbying the White House to prevent some A.I. models from being developed and widely shared because, they argued, they were too dangerous. But companies like Nvidia and Microsoft saw those A.I. models as a big business opportunity. At the end of July, Satya Nadella, chief executive of Microsoft, and Jensen Huang, then Nvidia’s chief executive, intervened. They emailed each other drafts of a letter saying those A.I. models should remain open, according to four people familiar with the discussions. When they asked other technology executives whether they’d like to sign on, two dozen companies quickly agreed before the letter became public. Over the next week, 200 more companies — including a chastened OpenAI — signed onto the letter . Dr. Amodei refused. Dr. Amodei has for years exasperated his peers with warnings about extreme risks of A.I., even as his company has built some of the most powerful A.I. systems in the world. Frustration has turned to hostility as Anthropic leaped into the lead in A.I. development, experienced stunning revenue growth and moved toward what is likely to be one of the largest initial public offerings ever later this month. Along the way, Anthropic — which has cultivated an image as a company that tries to do the right thing — has also gained a reputation for playing hardball with customers and competitors. It has cut some off from its service and lobbied against other companies’s free alternatives to its A.I. Over the last year, other technology companies and investors have organized to push back, according to more than 20 people in the technology industry, many of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to preserve their relationships with Anthropic. items.title: Nvidia Lost Its Founding C.E.O. Can It Keep Its Momentum?
items.summary: Throughout the years, tech giants have had mixed records after losing visionary founders who propelled their success. Successors with tech expertise helps.
items.full_text: Advice to Nvidia’s board: Choose a techie. As the chip giant’s directors seek a replacement to Jensen Huang, the history of successions at Silicon Valley companies suggests that the odds of long-term success are better with a person steeped in technology and product development rather than finance, sales or marketing. Replacing a founder is a defining moment for any company, whether it’s been planned for years or a sudden departure, whether the company is thriving or faltering. For Mr. Huang, Nvidia’s co-founder and former chief executive, the fall came remarkably quickly. He resigned on Thursday after the disclosure of affairs with a woman identified by U.S. intelligence as a Chinese spy and with an executive who reported to him. Nvidia’s business as the leading chip supplier to artificial intelligence data centers is flourishing. Mr. Huang’s hasty exit , analysts say, will have little near-term effect on the company’s business, despite a big stock-market reaction. (The company’s shares have fallen 14 percent in the last five days.) But the best tech leaders steer their companies toward opportunity. At Nvidia, founded in 1993, Mr. Huang recognized more than a decade ago that chips used mainly for image-processing in computer games could be repurposed as the hardware engines for A.I. software. It was a huge bet for the small company — and paid off. “You can coast on the founder’s work for years with good execution,” said Steve Blank, a Silicon Valley entrepreneur and investor, who is an adjunct professor at Stanford University. “But you can lack the founder’s vision to see over the horizon and identify what’s next. That’s why the best successors have a lot of technical acumen as well as business acumen.” Over the years, the results for tech companies replacing founding executives have been decidedly mixed. items.title: Howard Lutnick Took Softer Line on Nvidia as Calls for Tougher Controls Grew
items.summary: Critics say Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, and his department have shielded Nvidia as concerns have grown over A.I. chip sales to firms like Megaspeed.
items.full_text: There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence. Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce Department. Over the past year, Mr. Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales to Asia. That has drawn accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that the Commerce Department has become too cozy with Nvidia and its co-founder, Jensen Huang, and failed to adequately police the firm’s chip sales to China, in particular. The issue has exploded into public view in recent weeks with the revelations from The New York Times that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence agencies to be a Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang , was a top executive at a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. On Thursday, Mr. Huang announced that he was stepping down from the company , sending the company’s shares tumbling. The astonishing developments have thrust Mr. Lutnick into an uncomfortable spotlight and raised questions about whether he went too far in protecting Nvidia’s interests. And it has focused attention on whether the influence of Mr. Huang, an ally of President Trump’s and among the most high-profile and successful of American business leaders, kept the United States from moving faster to clamp down on sales of Nvidia chips to companies like Megaspeed. The stakes in the A.I. race between the United States and China are high. China hawks warn that allowing sales of advanced chips to that country is speeding its A.I. development and giving it an economic and military edge. Those who support the sales say they help U.S. technology maintain global leadership, while deterring China from developing rival products. As the head of a sprawling department that has control over enforcing restrictions on technology sales, Mr. Lutnick is best positioned to single-handedly shape whether China has access to American technology, including Nvidia’s. Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues given high priority and sent through specific channels.
